title: How to Keep Training for Inline Speed Skating Through Exam Season

scenes.heading: How to keep training for inline speed skating through exam season
scenes.sub: A small plan that protects your speed
scenes.narration: Exam season arrives every year, and it takes skaters by surprise every year. One week you are training five times. The next, you have four papers, a revision timetable, and a parent who would quite like you to stay off the road until it is over. So how do you keep your skating without failing your exams, or losing the speed you built all season? The answer is not doing both at full volume. It is a deliberately small plan that protects what fades fastest, and lets go of the rest.
scenes.chapter: Why exam season hurts your skating

scenes.heading: What holds, and what fades
scenes.narration: Start with what actually happens when training stops for a month. Your skating is not one quality. It is several, and they fade at very different rates. Technique is the most durable. The feel of a good push, an edge, the timing of a crossover, all of that stays in your nervous system for weeks. Strength and top speed are stubborn too, as long as they get a little stimulus. A few short, hard efforts keep them close. Aerobic fitness is the one that goes. The ability to hold a hard pace for twenty minutes is built by volume, and it leaves first when the volume stops. The good news is that it is also the quickest of the three to rebuild.

scenes.heading: Keep the frequency, cut the volume
bullets: Two 30 minute sessions beat one 90 minute session
Frequency keeps the movement familiar
A short session leaves your evening free for revision
The goal is maintenance, not progress
scenes.narration: If you take one idea from this video, take this one. When time collapses, protect how often you train, not how long. Two thirty minute sessions in a week will do far more for you than one ninety minute session, even though the long one has more skating in it. Frequency keeps the movement familiar and keeps your legs used to being asked. A long session also costs you more on the day, and during exams that means a worse evening of revision. Remember, an exam block is temporary. You are not trying to get faster. You are trying to come out the other side able to start training again, rather than starting over.

scenes.heading: A four week exam block
scenes.narration: Here is the shape that works for most skaters. Two skate sessions a week, thirty minutes each. One with short sprints, one with easy technique work. Put them on days with no paper the following morning. Add one fifteen minute strength session at home, and ten minutes of mobility most days, which is really for your back and hips after hours at a desk. In the week of your heaviest papers, drop to one skate session plus the mobility. That is not a failure. That is the plan working. Altogether it is about ninety minutes of training a week, and it is enough to hold most of what matters.

scenes.heading: The 30 minute session that protects your speed
bullets: 10 minutes of proper warm up
6 to 8 sprints of about 10 seconds, rolling start
A full easy lap, or two minutes, between sprints
5 minutes of easy skating to finish
scenes.narration: So what goes into that thirty minute session? Warm up properly for ten minutes, because a short session is no excuse for going hard on cold legs. Then do six to eight sprints of around ten seconds each, from a rolling start, with a full easy lap or a couple of minutes between them. Finish with five minutes of easy skating. Keep every sprint genuinely fast. The point is not to finish tired. It is to remind your body what fast feels like. And in your very worst weeks, cut it down to twenty minutes. An eight minute warm up, four sprints with long recoveries, a few easy laps, and home.

scenes.heading: Strength, sleep and sitting
bullets: 15 minutes of strength at home, no equipment
Cut the session, never the sleep
Train early, before the heat and before study
10 minutes of mobility in your study breaks
scenes.narration: For strength, you need no gym and no equipment. Squats, split squats, single leg balance, glute bridges, calf raises and a plank. Two or three rounds, done well rather than fast, and stop well short of soreness. Next, sleep comes before training. If something has to go on a given day, cut the session, not the sleep. Sleep is doing two jobs in exam season. It locks in what you studied, and it is the only recovery you are getting. The practical answer is to train early. Dawn sessions are cooler in an Indian summer, and you finish before revision starts. Finally, all that sitting shortens your hip flexors and stiffens your lower back. Ten minutes of mobility in a study break is enough to keep your low skating position available.

scenes.heading: If you have to stop completely
bullets: Clean and oil your bearings before the break
Wipe the frames, check axles, rotate the wheels
Store skates somewhere cool and dry
Spin every wheel before your first session back
scenes.narration: Some exam blocks leave no room at all, and a few weeks off is fine. What is not fine is coming back to skates that have gone backwards while you were revising. Before the gap, clean and oil your bearings so they are not sitting in grit and moisture for a month. A bottle of Speedslick Pro bearing oil and twenty minutes is all it takes. Wipe the frames, check the axles, rotate the wheels, and store everything somewhere dry and out of direct sun, not in a hot car boot or a damp cupboard. When you come back, spin each wheel before the first session. A rusty bearing will tell you straight away, and it is far better to find out at home than on the first corner.

scenes.heading: Coming back after the last paper
scenes.narration: After the final exam, the temptation is to go and do the session you have been dreaming about for a month. Please do not. Treating the first week back as a celebration is the most common way skaters lose a fortnight. Build up over two weeks instead. In week one, do three easy to moderate sessions and nothing maximal, and let your feet get used to the boots again, because skin that has been out of a speed boot for a month blisters easily. In week two, bring back one hard session and keep the rest steady. By week three, you are training normally.

scenes.heading: What not to do
bullets: Do not try to hold your normal training load
Do not train late at night to make up a session
Do not test yourself with a time trial
Do not change your setup during the gap
scenes.narration: A few things to avoid. Do not try to hold your normal training load, because something will give, and it is usually the exams, your sleep, or your knees. Do not train late at night to make up a missed session. Do not test yourself with a time trial on tired legs. It tells you nothing except that you are tired. And do not change anything on your skates during the gap. Save new wheels or a new frame for the comeback, so that if something feels odd, you know whether it is you or the gear.

scenes.heading: Protect frequency, not volume
scenes.sub: Full guide with the weekly plan at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: So, the short version. Protect frequency, not volume. Two short sessions and fifteen minutes of strength a week will hold most of your skating through an exam block. Train early, never trade sleep for a session, look after your bearings if you have to stop, and ramp back over two weeks, not one evening. The full guide, with the weekly plan and answers to common questions, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description. Good luck with your exams, and we will see you back on the road.
